name: Caro-Kann Defense: Karpov Variation
summary: Caro-Kann Defense Karpov Variation: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7, a solid setup preparing ...Ngf6 without the doubled pawns of 4...Nf6.
intro: The Karpov Variation of the Caro-Kann arises after 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7. This flexible knight move, favored by Anatoly Karpov, prepares ...Ngf6 so that the recapture on f6 does not damage Black's pawns, unlike 4...Nf6 5.Nxf6. The sharpest test is 5.Ng5, eyeing the sensitive e6 and f7 squares. Black aims for a super-solid if slightly passive structure, developing harmoniously with ...e6, ...Bd6 or ...Be7, ...c5, and completing a safe king position while accepting a modest space concession.
line: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nd7 Ng5 Ngf6 Bd3 e6 N1f3 h6 Ne4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The point of 4...Nd7 is structural. By developing the queen's knight first, Black prepares ...Ngf6 so that a capture on f6 can be met with ...Nxf6, keeping the pawns intact instead of accepting the doubled f-pawns of the Bronstein-Larsen. The result is a resilient, symmetrical-looking structure with pawns on c6 and e6 that is hard to crack. Black concedes a little space and time but obtains a durable position with clear developing moves: the bishops go to d6 or e7 and b7 or d7, and the ...c5 break frees the game and challenges White's d4 pawn later on.

White's compensation is a lead in development and lasting space, which encourages aggressive setups. The critical 5.Ng5 immediately probes e6 and f7, and the whole line is famous for sacrificial ideas against a prematurely weakened kingside, which is exactly why ...h6 must be timed with care. In slower handling White plays Bd3, Ngf3, O-O and Qe2, aiming for a small pull based on space and easier piece activity. If Black is allowed to complete development and play ...c5 under good conditions, the position equalizes; if not, White's initiative can become dangerous.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The sharp main line runs 5.Ng5 Ngf6 6.Bd3 e6 7.N1f3 h6 8.Ne4, when White retreats the knight and keeps a pleasant space edge with straightforward development to follow. The move ...h6 must be played only when the sacrifices on e6 and f7 do not work, since a careless ...h6 can invite exactly those blows. After the knight steps back to e4, Black continues with ...Nxe4 or ...Bd6, ...c5, ...O-O, and ...b6, reaching a solid middlegame. Quieter tries such as 5.Nf3 or 5.Bc4 also exist, steering toward calmer positional battles.

A recurring theme is the trade of knights on e4 or f6 and the timing of Black's freeing ...c5. If Black exchanges a pair of knights and achieves ...c5, the light-squared bishop can develop actively and the structure becomes very sound. White, for his part, tries to prevent easy equality by keeping pieces on, pressing with Qe2 and Rd1, and probing the slightly passive Black position. Endgames tend to be comfortable for Black thanks to the healthy pawns, so White usually seeks to keep the middlegame tension and exploit the temporary spatial and developmental lead.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Caro-Kann, named for Horatio Caro and Marcus Kann in the late nineteenth century, is one of the most solid replies to 1.e4. The 4...Nd7 system was employed with great success by Anatoly Karpov, who valued its rock-solid structure and low-risk profile, and it is sometimes also linked historically to Steinitz. Karpov used it to neutralize sharp attacking players by reaching resilient positions where Black could gradually equalize. It remains a mainstay at every level, prized by those who want a dependable, strategically clear defense that avoids the structural concessions of the alternative 4...Nf6 lines.
